question: Which of the following medications is an antibody against the interleukin-6 (IL-6) receptor?
explanation: Interleukin-6 (IL-6) is a cytokine that has been found to be significantly up-regulated during infection and inflammation. IL-6 is a pleiotropic, pro- inflammatory cytokine, that is mainly produced by T cells and monocytes/macrophages. IL-6 induces proliferation and differentiation of T cells as well as the terminal differentiation of B cells. In multiple experimental autoimmune uveitis models. IL-6 has been shown to he essential for inducing inflammation. IL-6 levels have been found to be significantly elevated in ocular fluids derived from diabetic macular edema, retinal vein occlusion, and refractory/chronic uveitis patients. Furthermore, multiple studies have shown amelioration of chronic inflammation with blockade of IL-6. Tocilizumab is a humanized monoclonal antibody against the IL-6 receptor and is currently approved and widely used for the treatment of rheumatoid arthritis. The Study of the Safety, Tolerability, and Bioactivity of Tocilizumab On Patients With Non-infectious uveitis (STOP- uveitis) found repeated intravenous administrations of Tocilizumab were well tolerated and effective in improving visual acuity and reducing vitreous haze and retinal edema in patients with noninfectious posterior, intermediate, or panuveitis. In addition, multiple reports have been published elucidating the effectiveness of reducing inflammation in patients with juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA)-associated uveitis, refractory to treatment by other medications. explanation: The clinical vignette presents a young, myopic, healthy woman who presents with distortion of vision. The fundus photo shows focal lesions some of which have progressed to atrophic/pigmentary chorioretinal scars. The FA shows early hyperfluorescence with late staining of the lesions. These properties are characteristic of the white dot syndrome (WDS) known as punctate inner choroidopathy. PIC and MFC (another WDS) are considered to be related entities. Both affect young myopic women and eventually involve both eyes. A diagnosis of PIC is made when the inflammatory lesions are small (100-200 microns) and confined to the posterior pole with minimal vitreous reaction. In contrast, more diffuse disease with larger lesions and vitreous reaction characterize MFC. POHS (NOT a WDS) is characterized by "punched out" mid-peripheral lesions, peripapillary atrophy, and always the absence of vitritis. Like PIC and MFC, a common cause of vision loss in POHS patients is due to choroidal neovascularization. The WDS known as AZOOR typically also presents in young women who complain of photopsias and progressive visual field loss. The field loss typically begins as enlargement of the blind spot. The early lesions of AZOOR are multiple small white-gray dots without RE atrophy/hyperpigmentation. Several months later, these lesions develop RE atrophy/hyperpigmentation which can sometimes resemble the bone spicules of retinitis pigmentosa. explanation: This fundus montage shows zonal areas of atrophy and hyperpigmentation of the RPE along with multiple, small white dots sprinkled throughout the fundus. This fundus appearance along with the clinical history of a young, otherwise healthy woman who initially experienced photopsias, is characteristic for acute zonal occult outer retinopathy (AZOOR). AZOOR is one of the white-dot syndromes (WDS), and during its initial presentation (i.e. multiple small white-gray dots without RE atrophy/hyperpigmentation), is most likely confused with MEWDS (multiple evanescent white dot syndrome). Like many of the other WDS, AZOOR presents with photopsias in the vast majority of cases (>75%). Similar to MEWDS. it can be occasionally associated with a prodromal flu-like illness and usually occurs in women. AZOOR is unilateral 60% of time on initial presentation. However unlike MEWDS, AZOOR can ultimately involve the fellow eye in 60% of unilateral cases (i.e. ~75% of all cases are bilateral). Males presenting with AZOOR are more commonly affected bilaterally. In contrast. MEWDS usually resolves completely within 3 months without any visual damage and is rarely bilateral. Most AZOOR patients develop acute visual loss followed by stabilization after approximately 6 months. Typically, patients complain of their vision loss in terms of visual field defects which correspond to the areas of RPE atrophy that progressively develop after the acute episode. The RPE hyperpigmentation can resemble the bone spicules of retinitis pigmentosa (R) and syphilitic chorioretinitis. Indeed, the differential diagnosis of AZOOR is: the other WDS (especially MEWDS), RP, syphilis, diffuse unilateral subacute neuroretinitis, and carcinoma-associated retinopathy. explanation: Birdshot retinochoriodopathy (BSCR) is characterized by hypopigmented choroidal lesions ¼ to ½ optic disc diameter in size, clustered around the optic nerve, radiating towards the periphery, nearly always involving the inferior and nasal peripapillary area, in a pattern similar to the gunshot spatter from birdshot. This disease presents predominately in Caucasian women past the fourth decade of life. It is highly correlated with the HLA-A29 gene, with a sensitivity of 96% and specificity of 93%. Presenting symptoms can include decreased vision, floaters, nyctalopia, dyschromatopsia, glare, and photopsias. Anterior segment findings may be minimal or lacking and varying degrees of vitritis may be present. Indocyanine green angiography (ICG) discloses multiple hypofluorescent spots, which are typically more numerous than those apparent on slit lamp examination or fluorescein angiography. ERG findings typically show prolonged 30 Hz flicker implicit times. In addition, BSCR has markedly diminished "b" waves (i.e. abnormally-functioning Mueller and bipolar cells) compared to "a" wave (i.e. photoreceptors) amplitudes. The disease is usually incompletely responsive to steroids alone and requires the early use immunomodulatory therapies. explanation: The patient is presenting with acute posterior multifocal placoid pigment epitheliopathy (APMPPE). Patients present in the second to third decade with rapid loss of vision and/or paracentral scotomata in one (uncommon) or both (frequent) eyes due to multiple postequatorial, gray-white, placoid lesions at the level of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) with disruption of the overlying photoreceptors. On fluorescein angiography, these lesions block early and stain late. Vitreous cell is present in approximately 50% of patients, but anterior chamber inflammation is typically absent. There is often an antecedent flu like illness. Other associated systemic findings and diseases include scleritis, thyroiditis, CNS vasculitis, erythema nodosum, ulcerative colitis, sarcoidosis, and other systemic vasculitides (e.g., GPA, PAN). Prognosis is excellent with lesions beginning to fade after a few days. Over the course of weeks, the lesions are replaced by areas of partially depigmented RPE with pigment clumping. Despite the irregular appearance, the overlying photoreceptors tend to reconstitute with resolution of visual acuity, although some patients will be able to identify persistent paracentral scotomata. There is no evidence for treatment with corticosteroids to alter the natural course of the disease, however some will treat for lesions close to fixation. Because of the association between APMPPE and CNS vasculitis, neurologic symptoms require an emergent workup. If untreated, CNS vasculitis has a mortality of 95%, 46% if treated with corticosteroids, and 8% if treated with a combination of corticosteroids and a cytotoxic agent. WRONG ANSWERS: o (Choice A): Observation would be an appropriate choice for a patient who is not exhibiting neurologic symptoms concerning for a CNS vasculitis. If untreated, CNS vasculitis has a mortality of 95%, 46% if treated with corticosteroids, and 8% if treated with a combination of corticosteroids and a cytotoxic agent. o (Choice C): There is no evidence for the use of oral corticosteroids in altering the course of disease in APMPPE. Furthermore, topical steroids would not be an appropriate choice given the lack of anterior chamber inflammation. o (Choice D): Intravitreal injection of foscarnet would be an appropriate treatment for rapid induction of heretic necrotizing retinitis (e.g., acute retinal necrosis, ARN, or posterior outer progressive retinopathy, PORN). Treatment typically includes induction with IV acyclovir (10 mg/kg TID) or oral valacylovir (2 grams TID) for 10-14 days with or without the addition of intravitreal foscarnet. explanation: This patient exhibits the classic findings of autoimmune peripheral ulcerative keratitis (PUK). Peripheral ulcerative keratitis usually presents with a unilateral, crescent-shaped destructive lesion of the peripheral corneal stroma with an overlying epithelial defect. The most common systemic association is rheumatoid arthritis. The primary treatment for acute disease control is systemic corticosteroids and an additional immunomodulatory agent is often started concurrently. It has been reported in the literature thatthe mortalitv rate in untreated rheumatoid arthritis patients with PUK/necrotizing scleritis is approximately 50% over a 10-year period. The new-onset occurrence of PUK can be considered a sign of active systemic vasculitis and a change in systemic immunomodulatory therapy is appropriate at this time. Disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs) are a group of medications commonly used in patients with rheumatoid arthritis. They have been found to be very effective in reducing inflammation in patients with rheumatoid arthritis. Methotrexate (MTX) is considered as first-line therapy; sulfasalazine (SSZ) or leflunomide can be substituted if there are contraindications to MTX. Azathioprine is a purine nucleoside analog which acts as an antimetabolite by interfering with DNA and RNA synthesis. Prior to initiating therapy with azathioprine, thiopurine S-methyltransferase activity should be assessed to determine patient candidacy for azaithioprine as well as individualize patient doses. Azathioprine is contraindicated in patients with a history of hypersensitivity to the drug and in patients with rheumatoid arthritis previously treated with alkylating agents, due to the potentially high risk of neoplasia. Adalimumab is a biologic that inhibits the action of tumor necrosis factor- alpha (TNF-a). TNF- a plays a major role in the induction of inflammatory cytokines, therefore blocking TNF-a can significantly reduce inflammation. Biologic therapy is mostly used when patients with active rheumatoid arthritis do not have a satisfactory response to traditional DMARDs. explanation: A wide range of organisms can enter the eye following ocular trauma and cause endophthalmitis. Identification of the causative pathogen(s) is an important step in the management of infectious endophthalmitis. Most cases of post-traumatic endophthalmitis are bacterial, usually Staphylococcus species. Bacillus infections are commonly seen in the setting of intraocular foreign body and/or wounds contaminated with soil. Fungal endophthalmitis is a relatively rare complication of open globe injury. There is usually a latent period of weeks-to-months in fungal endophthalmitis, and patients often present with minimal ocular discomfort. explanation: Toxic anterior segment syndrome (TASS) is a sterile, non-infectious, acute, postoperative anterior segment inflammation that is caused by a noninfectious substance that enters the anterior segment, resulting in toxic damage to intraocular tissues. The etiology of TASS may be multi-factorial with numerous potential causes: o Bacterial endotoxins or particulate contamination of balanced salt solutions. o Intraocular irrigating solutions with abnormal pH, osmolarity or ionic composition. o Denatured ophthalmic viscosurgical devices (OVD). o Intraocular medications (antibiotics in the irrigation solutions or intracameral antibiotics). o Topical ointments. o Inadequate sterilization of surgical instruments and tubing. o Inadequate flushing of instruments between cases resulting in build-up of OVD. o Preservatives in medications used intraoperatively. o Metallic precipitate When treating these cases, it is important to make sure that the patient has TASS and not endophthalmitis. The typical hallmark of TASS is an inflammatory process that starts within 24 hours of cataract surgery, whereas infectious endophthalmitis takes several days to present. However, in the "real world", their are no absolutes. The indications for vitreous tap and injection of antibiotics are guided by clinical clues or if the treating ophthalmologist is uncomfortable making the diagnosis of TASS. In TASS, patients usually complain of blurred vision, mild ocular pain and eye redness. In severe cases of TASS, it is not uncommon to see fibrin formation in the anterior chamber and/or on the surface of the iris and intraocular lens. The syndrome can also result in permanent iris damage, which may cause a dilated pupil; an irregular pupil that constricts and dilates poorly; and/or potential trabecular meshwork damage. The inflammation is limited to the anterior segment of the eye, is always Gram stain and culture negative, and usually improves with steroid treatment. The primary differential diagnosis is infectious endophthalmitis. With infectious endophthalmitis, onset is usually between 2 and 7 days after surgery. Once an infectious etiology has been ruled out, treatment for TASS consists of intense topical corticosteroids drops. After treatment, if the insult is mild, patients will tend to improve fairly quickly. There will be rapid clearing of the inflammation, the cornea will clear, and there will be no resulting permanent vision loss. explanation: Most primary central nervous lymphomas (PCNLs) are non-Hodgkin B-Lymphocyte lymphomas. The disease is considered primary intraocular lymphoma (PIOL), or primary vitreoretinal lymphoma (PVRL), if at the time of diagnosis, it is limited to the eye and there is no other central nervous system involvement. Up to 25 percent of patients with PCNL have ocular involvement and some experts believe that in the setting of a pre- existing diagnosis of PCNL, diagnosing intraocular involvement can be done based off clinical findings and a biopsy of an ophthalmic site is unnecessary. In the absence of known central nervous system lymphoma, intraocular biopsy is necessary to confirm the diagnosis of PIOL in the appropriate clinical context. Cytological identification of lymphoma cells within the eye via vitreous, retinal, or sub-retinal biopsy remains the gold standard in the diagnosis of PIOL. Most often, vitreous biopsy via pars plan vitrectomy is undertaken. The atypical lymphoid cells are usually large and pleomorphic, with scant basophilic cytoplasm and large nuclei. Many studies have shown a high-false negative rate of vitreous biopsies sent for cytological examination to confirm the diagnosis of PIOL. Vitreous specimens may not always contain neoplastic cells and, thus, be negative for a diagnosis of lymphoma. This might especially be the case if there is minimal vitreous involvement by the PIOL cells or the cells have degenerated due their inherent fragility. In addition, atypical lymphoma cells in the vitreous often admix with reactive lymphocytes, necrotic cells and debris, further adding to the difficulty of diagnosis. Adjunctive testing of the vitreous specimen is often necessary to confirm the diagnosis of PIOL. Cytokine Analysis B-cell malignancies have been found to secrete high levels of the cytokine interleukin-10 (IL-10), an immunosupressive cytokine. Whereas, inflammatory conditions are associated with high levels of interleukin-6, a pro-inflammatory cytokine. Various studies have shown that PIOL can exhibit high IL-10 levels with IL-10:IL-6 ratios greater than 1.0 being suggestive of PIOL. One study at the National Eye Institute, found the IL-10:IL-6 ratio in the vitreous of the cases of PIOL correctly identified 74.7% of the cases, with a sensitivity of 74.3% and a specificity of 75.0%. Molecular Analysis Polymerase chain reaction (PC can be used to show a monoclonal proliferation of malignant B cell lymphoma cells and immunoglobulin heavy chain (IgH) rearrangement testing analyzes the clonality of the antibodies being produced. In cases of a neoplastic proliferation of lymphocytes, a monoclonal IgH gene rearrangement is primarily produced. In contrast, non-neoplastic proliferation of lymphocytes, as seen in inflammatory processes, produces a multiple different (polyclonal) IgH rearrangements. A feature of diffuse large B-cell lymphoma arising in immune-privileged sites is a high frequency of Myeloid Differentiation Primary Response Gene 88 (MYD88) mutations. Recently, multiple published studies have identified mutations in the MYD88 gene in up to 87% of vitrectomy samples of patients with a known diagnosis of PIOL. This mutation can be detected via PCR and is specific enough that many experts consider the presence of this mutation a positive diagnosis of PIOL. Immunophenotyping Immunohistochemistry and flow cytometry are able to identify lymphoma cells and demonstrate their monoclonality by B-cell and plasma cell markers and kappa or lambda light chain restriction. A typical vitreous flow cytometric panel includes a large number of Band T-cell markers, as well as kappa and lambda light-chain markers. A kappa:lambda light-chain ratio of >3 or <0.6 is useful as a marker for monoclonality as the usual ratio in heterogeneous inflammatory reactions is usually close to 1. JXG is a type of non-Langerhan's cell histiocytosis; histopathology of a skin lesion would show Touton giant cells and large foamy histiocytes.
